title: Three pillars
hookLine: Simon the Just: the world stands on Torah, worship and acts of kindness (Pirkei Avot 1:2)
tomorrow: if i'm only for myself, what am i? who asked that, and why?

cards: A wobbly café table has four legs. A three-legged stool never wobbles, even on a crooked floor. So, which three things hold up the world?

An old Jewish book of sayings, Pirkei Avot, gives an answer in its second saying. Simon the Just, called one of the last of the Great Assembly, used to say: the world stands on three things. On Torah, the teaching.
On avodah, the service of worship in the Temple. And on gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness. Three legs.
A steady world. Except for one problem.

teach.b: Here's the puzzle. One of the three legs was the Temple service, the offerings in Jerusalem. And the Temple was destroyed.
So what is the world standing on now? A story from Avot de-Rabbi Natan answers it.

Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai was walking out of Jerusalem with his student, Rabbi Joshua, and they passed the Temple in ruins. Joshua cried out: woe to us, the place where Israel's wrongs were atoned for is gone.
Yohanan said: my son, don't grieve. We have another atonement just like it. Which?
And he quoted the prophet Hosea, in the King James words: "For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice." Look at the Hebrew. The word Hosea uses for mercy is chesed, the same word inside gemilut chasadim.
The third leg was holding the weight all along. This is a real turn in Jewish life.
The rabbis taught that prayer is the service of the heart, and that kindness carries what the altar used to carry.
It's one reason visiting the sick, feeding a guest and comforting mourners count as holy work in Judaism, not as extras next to it. When one pillar falls, the others take the load.

how: Jews study Pirkei Avot, the Sayings of the Fathers, often on Shabbat afternoons in the weeks after Passover; acts of loving-kindness, such as visiting the sick and comforting mourners, are treated as religious duties.

games.q: the three pillars and the ruins: tap the pairs.
p: kindness atones like the altar did

s: to the rabbis, kindness was a nice extra next to the real religious duties
it's one of the three pillars, and Yohanan ben Zakkai said it atones as the Temple offerings did.
the Hebrew word in Hosea's 'I desired mercy' is chesed
the same word that sits inside gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness.
Simon the Just says the world stands on Torah alone
he names three: Torah, worship, and acts of loving-kindness.

games.q: you're Rabbi Joshua, standing at the ruins. the place of atonement is gone. what does your teacher Yohanan tell you?
o: don't grieve: acts of loving-kindness atone just as the offerings did.
the world can't stand now; wait until the Temple is rebuilt.
study harder; Torah alone can hold up the whole world.
games.why: in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, Yohanan points to kindness and quotes Hosea: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice.

practice: Choose one person who could use an act of kindness this week, and name, to yourself, the kind thing you could do.
Then name what usually stops you, the awkwardness, the busy day, and decide when and how you'll do it anyway: if this happens, then I'll do that.

wordCard.voice: Three pillars: Torah, worship and acts of loving-kindness, the three things Simon the Just says the world stands on.

orig.note: Hebrew: the doing of kindnesses, Simon the Just's third pillar.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: three pillars, and the kindness one still standing. Day one of the sayings of the Fathers.
